paragraphs: Structured prediction involves choosing outputs with internal structure, such as a sequence of labels or a dependency parse. The inference procedure determines which output a learned model selects. This paper asks how replacing exact inference with an approximation affects learning error, rather than judging the approximation only by how closely it reproduces an exact inference result.

The analysis compares estimation and approximation errors for both underestimate and overestimate models. Considering these sources of error together matters because accuracy within the inference procedure is only one part of the learning problem. The stated result is that approximate inference could perform as well as exact inference from the perspective of learning errors; it does not establish that every approximation will do so.

The error analysis also motivates a new margin for existing learning algorithms, connecting the theoretical comparison to a concrete training change. Evaluations on text classification, sequential labeling, and dependency parsing support the usefulness of approximate inference and show benefits from the proposed margin.
neurips-2017-a-learning-error-analysis-f.tldr: An analysis of structured prediction shows that approximate inference can match exact inference in learning error and motivates an improved training margin.

paragraphs: Relational reasoning concerns how entities and their properties relate to one another. This paper introduces Relation Networks as a module that can be added to existing neural networks to help solve problems requiring this kind of reasoning. The motivation is to give relationships a dedicated computational component instead of leaving the entire burden to other network components.

The authors evaluate networks augmented with this module on visual questions in CLEVR, text questions in the bAbI suite, and reasoning about dynamical physical systems. On CLEVR, they report performance above both the previous state of the art and human performance. A separate study using Sort-of-CLEVR shows that powerful convolutional networks struggle with relational questions and gain the relevant capacity when augmented with Relation Networks.

The architectural contribution is a reusable way to equip convolutions, LSTMs, and multilayer perceptrons with relational computation. The reported findings support assigning that work to a specialized module, which can reduce overall network complexity while improving the ability to reason about relationships.
neurips-2017-a-simple-neural-network-mod.tldr: Relation Networks add a reusable relational reasoning module to neural networks, with strong results on visual, textual, and physical reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods improve a control policy using an estimated direction of improvement. In some applications, learning begins with a policy that already works well, and trying a worse policy may be unacceptable. This paper studies how to choose updates with that concern in mind, focusing on both the amount of data collected and the size of the policy change.

The batch size determines how many samples are used to estimate the gradient direction. The step size determines how far the policy parameters move along that direction. The authors propose methods that optimize these two choices jointly, addressing a decision that receives less attention when the focus is only on selecting a step size.

The methods provide high-probability guarantees of improved policy performance after each update. That qualification matters: the stated safety property is probabilistic, rather than an unconditional promise about every update. Numerical simulations examine the methods' behavior, complementing the theory and illustrating the role of jointly selecting sampling effort and update size.
neurips-2017-adaptive-batch-size-for-saf.tldr: Jointly choosing batch size and step size gives policy gradient updates with high-probability guarantees of performance improvement.

paragraphs: ADMM uses a quadratic penalty to enforce equality constraints, and its performance can depend strongly on the penalty's size. This paper develops an adaptive penalty scheme for ADMM and a linearized variant. The methods handle structured, nonsmooth objectives in both deterministic and stochastic optimization settings.

The central idea is to adapt to a local sharpness property of the objective, rather than adjusting the penalty solely through conditions checked on successive iterates. With sharpness described by an exponent θ between zero and one, the stated iteration complexities are Õ(1/ε^(1−θ)) for deterministic optimization and Õ(1/ε^(2(1−θ))) for stochastic optimization. Here, ε is the target accuracy and the notation suppresses a logarithmic factor.

These conditional bounds improve on standard ADMM with a fixed penalty and do not require smoothness or strong convexity. Experiments also show convergence comparable to, and sometimes much faster than, ADMM with a carefully tuned fixed penalty. The contribution therefore combines a structural explanation for faster convergence with evidence that adaptive penalization can be practically useful.
neurips-2017-admm-without-a-fixed-penalt.tldr: An ADMM penalty scheme adapted to local objective sharpness improves conditional convergence bounds and performs competitively with carefully tuned fixed penalties.

paragraphs: This paper studies low-rank matrix approximation when error means the number of entries that disagree with the original matrix. The size of each disagreement does not matter. That objective is useful when data has no underlying distance measure, but finding the best rank-k approximation under it is NP-hard.

For k greater than one, the authors give a polynomial-time algorithm with a tradeoff between rank and error. It produces a matrix of rank O(k log(n/k)) whose disagreement count is at most O(k² log(n/k)) times the best rank-k error. The guarantee therefore allows both extra rank and extra error. The authors identify it as the first provable guarantee they know for this case, even with such flexibility.

For rank one, they obtain a (2+ε)-approximation in sublinear time. For binary matrices, the factor improves to 1+O(ψ), where ψ is the optimal error divided by the number of nonzero input entries. When that ratio is small, the approximation factor approaches one, giving especially strong accuracy for this particular regime.
neurips-2017-approximation-algorithms-fo.tldr: New algorithms approximate low-rank matrices by minimizing entry disagreements, with guarantees for higher ranks and sublinear-time results for rank one.

paragraphs: A probabilistic graphical model represents conditional independence relationships among variables using a graph. Learning a sparse graph means identifying a relatively small set of dependencies that describes the distribution. This paper addresses that task for continuous, non-Gaussian data, extending beyond the discrete or Gaussian settings that restrict many existing structure-learning algorithms.

The method uses transport maps, which deterministically transform one probability measure into another. Its central mechanism is a connection between sparsity in these maps and sparsity in the distribution's graph. Exploiting that relationship provides a route from a representation of the probability distribution to an estimate of which variables remain conditionally dependent.

The approach matters because a more realistic description of a non-Gaussian distribution can support a better estimate of its dependence structure. Sparse graphs can also make inference faster, improve sampling methods, and reveal important relationships between variables. The contribution is an algorithm built around this transport-map connection, allowing sparse graphical modeling to address distributions beyond the usual Gaussian framework.
neurips-2017-beyond-normality-learning-s.tldr: The paper learns sparse dependence graphs for continuous non-Gaussian distributions by exploiting their connection to sparse transport maps.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function that explains an expert's demonstrated behavior. Many approaches require specifying in advance a space of candidate reward functions. This paper introduces a model-free method that instead constructs a suitable reward space using a condition associated with optimal policies.

The starting point is that an optimal policy must have a zero policy gradient. The algorithm generates basis functions spanning a subspace of rewards that make this gradient vanish. This narrows the search to rewards compatible with that first-order condition. Within the resulting subspace, a second-order criterion selects the reward that most strongly penalizes deviations from the expert's policy.

The distinction between these stages matters: making a gradient vanish supplies the candidate space, while the second-order criterion supplies a preference among its rewards. The authors develop the method for finite domains and extend it to continuous ones. They compare it empirically with other inverse reinforcement learning methods in Taxi, Linear Quadratic Gaussian, and Car on the Hill environments.
neurips-2017-compatible-reward-inverse-r.tldr: A model-free inverse reinforcement learning method constructs candidate rewards from policy-gradient conditions and selects among them using a second-order criterion.

paragraphs: Robust linear regression aims to recover a relationship even when some response values are corrupted. An important setting permits corruption in a constant fraction of those values, with potentially unbounded corruption magnitudes. This paper introduces CRR, an estimator designed to combine computational efficiency with statistical consistency in that challenging setting.

Consistency means that estimation can approach the true model as the amount of data grows. The authors present CRR as the first efficient estimator with a proof of that property for dense, unbounded corruptions, resolving an open problem identified in earlier work. Their analysis uses a two-stage proof and examines the stability of ordered lists, a technical ingredient they suggest may have broader interest.

The empirical comparison includes extended Lasso and TORRENT. CRR achieves comparable or better model recovery while running an order of magnitude faster in the reported comparisons. Thus, the contribution joins an asymptotic recovery guarantee with practical evidence of improved runtime, rather than treating robustness only as tolerance of corrupted observations.
neurips-2017-consistent-robust-regressio.tldr: CRR combines efficient robust regression with a consistency guarantee under dense, unbounded response corruption and strong empirical runtime results.

paragraphs: Hashing supports image retrieval by representing images with binary codes. This paper asks how to make those codes better reflect semantic information available during training. Its guiding assumption is that useful learned codes should also be well suited to classification, so their training should account for class prediction as well as relationships between image pairs.

The proposed deep supervised discrete hashing method combines pairwise label information and classification information in one network stream. It directly constrains the final layer's outputs to be binary codes. This makes the discrete representation part of the optimization itself, aligning the learned output with the form of the code used for retrieval.

Because the code constraints are discrete, the authors optimize the objective using alternating minimization. Experiments on benchmark datasets report improvements over the state-of-the-art methods used in the comparison. The stated findings support combining these two forms of supervision with direct binary constraints, showing that classification information can help shape codes for image search under the paper's approach.
neurips-2017-deep-supervised-discrete-ha.tldr: A deep hashing method learns binary image codes directly using both pairwise labels and classification information, improving benchmark retrieval results.

paragraphs: Iterations of optimization algorithms can resemble neural network layers, suggesting that training data might be used to learn more effective replacements for those iterations. This paper develops that connection for Bayesian sparse estimation algorithms. These algorithms promote solutions with few active components and can involve several nested optimization loops.

The authors show parallels between those multi-loop procedures and gated networks such as LSTMs. In particular, they examine how latent variables evolve across different time scales during optimization and how those trajectories correspond to activations in networks designed to model sequences adaptively. This gives a structural reason to use more sophisticated recurrent architectures for the estimation problem.

The resulting sparse estimation system, when supplied with training data, can efficiently estimate optimal solutions in regimes where other algorithms fail. Reported applications include direction-of-arrival estimation and recovery of 3D geometry. The paper also suggests that the same principles could inform learned replacements for a broader range of multi-loop algorithms, presenting that extension as a possibility rather than an established result.
neurips-2017-from-bayesian-sparsity-to-g.tldr: Connections between Bayesian sparse estimation and gated recurrent networks lead to a learned estimator that succeeds in challenging sparse recovery regimes.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data into progressively finer groups. This paper evaluates such hierarchies using an explicit cost function, allowing algorithms to be judged by how close their cost is to the best possible value. Its theoretical setting is a hierarchical stochastic blockmodel, a random graph model with hierarchical structure.

In certain regimes of that model, combining a singular value decomposition approach with particular linkage methods gives a constant-factor approximation to the clustering objective. A second approach combines semidefinite relaxations for balanced cuts with recursive sparsest cuts. It achieves a constant-factor guarantee over slightly broader regimes and in a semi-random setting where an adversary can remove edges from the generated graph.

These guarantees depend on the stated graph settings, making the model assumptions central to the result. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the SVD-based method achieves lower costs than widely used heuristics. For problems involving multiclass classification, it also produces better classification accuracy, linking improvement in the clustering objective to a downstream task.
neurips-2017-hierarchical-clustering-bey.tldr: Under hierarchical random graph assumptions, spectral and semidefinite approaches achieve constant-factor clustering guarantees, with empirical benefits for the spectral method.

paragraphs: Information about how an image was captured can help interpret it. For crowd counting, camera angle and height provide clues about people's appearance and scale. This paper proposes an adaptive convolutional neural network that uses such side information to change its convolution filters according to the current scene context.

A learned sub-network takes the side information as input and generates filter weights. The possible weights are modeled as a low-dimensional manifold within the much larger space of all filter weights. This gives the network a structured way to adapt its feature extraction to known variations, including perspective, noise level, or blur parameters.

The authors test the approach on crowd counting, corrupted digit recognition, and image deblurring. Their experiments show improvements over a plain convolutional network with a similar parameter count. They also collect a crowd counting dataset with ground-truth camera angle and height because existing datasets lack those annotations. The results support making contextual information directly influence image processing through adaptive filters.
neurips-2017-incorporating-side-informat.tldr: Adaptive convolution generates filters from side information such as camera perspective or noise level, improving results on three vision tasks.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether one visual representation can support recognition across very different kinds of images, including dog breeds, stop signs, and digits. The central challenge is to share what a network learns while still accommodating the differences between these visual domains. A representation that works across them would make shared learning useful for a broader range of image problems.

The authors develop a tunable deep network that uses residual adapter modules to adjust its behavior for different domains on the fly. The approach draws inspiration from networks that predict another network’s parameters. The adapters provide a way to steer a shared architecture toward particular kinds of images. The authors report substantial parameter sharing while maintaining, or sometimes improving, the accuracy of domain-specific representations. This finding suggests that extensive sharing can coexist with effective specialization.

The paper also introduces the Visual Decathlon Challenge to evaluate representations across ten distinct visual domains. Its emphasis is on recognizing images well across the full collection of domains. This makes broad, consistent recognition a central evaluation objective alongside the architectural goal of sharing parameters.
neurips-2017-learning-multiple-visual-do.tldr: Residual adapters let a shared visual network adjust to diverse image domains while maintaining or improving domain-specific accuracy.

paragraphs: Multiplicative weights update maintains a probability distribution over actions and adjusts each action's weight according to its cost. This paper studies its behavior in congestion games when agents use constant learning rates. The central question is whether repeated updates settle at an exact Nash equilibrium or continue moving indefinitely.

For the update that multiplies an action's probability by 1−εC and then normalizes, the authors prove convergence to exact Nash equilibria for arbitrary admissible constant learning rates. Here, C is the action's cost and ε is the learning rate; admissibility includes keeping the multiplicative factor positive. The result therefore permits constant rates without asserting that every numerical choice is valid.

A closely related rule replaces that factor with (1−ε)^C, yet its behavior can be radically different. Even a load balancing game with two agents and two strategies can exhibit limit cycles or chaos under this variant. The comparison shows that seemingly similar cost-based updates can have fundamentally different long-term dynamics.
neurips-2017-multiplicative-weights-upda.tldr: One constant-rate multiplicative weights rule converges in congestion games, while a closely related rule can produce cycles or chaos.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn several related functions represented by weighted automata. Its starting question is what makes the corresponding learning tasks related in a way an algorithm can exploit. The authors answer by considering how much of an underlying representation the automata can share.

To express that relationship, they introduce vector-valued weighted automata. A single model represents multiple task outputs, providing a formal setting for shared structure. They then develop a spectral learning algorithm for this model. Learning the tasks jointly enforces the discovery of a common representation space, making sharing an explicit property of the learning procedure.

This matters because the method connects a definition of task relatedness with a concrete mechanism for learning related tasks together. The authors provide theoretical motivation for the benefits and demonstrate them on synthetic and real-world datasets. The stated contribution is therefore both a modeling framework for shared automaton representations and an algorithm whose multitask benefits are supported by analysis and experiments.
neurips-2017-multitask-spectral-learning.tldr: A spectral algorithm learns related weighted automata jointly by representing their tasks in a shared vector-valued model.

paragraphs: Large matrix multiplications can be distributed across workers, but slow or failed workers can delay the final result. This paper considers a master coordinating workers that each store portions of the input matrices. It designs their intermediate computations using coding theory so that the master can reconstruct the output from enough completed responses.

The proposed polynomial codes achieve the optimal recovery threshold: the smallest number of workers the master must wait for in the studied setting. Their algebraic structure turns reconstruction into polynomial interpolation, which can be solved efficiently. This links the allocation of redundant computation to a tractable procedure for recovering the final matrix product.

The authors report an improvement in the order of the recovery threshold over prior approaches and establish optimality for additional metrics, including computation latency and communication load. They also extend the code to distributed convolution and show order-wise optimality there. The contribution is a coordinated design of worker computations and output recovery that uses redundancy optimally under the paper's distributed computation setting.
neurips-2017-polynomial-codes-an-optimal.tldr: Polynomial codes optimally reduce how many workers must finish distributed matrix multiplication and enable efficient reconstruction through polynomial interpolation.

paragraphs: Planning under partial observability means choosing actions without directly observing the full state of the environment. QMDP-net addresses this problem through a recurrent policy network that connects a model to a planning algorithm. The network therefore incorporates the structure of a planning solution into a trainable architecture.

The architecture is fully differentiable, allowing the combined system to be trained end to end. It represents policies for a parameterized collection of tasks, and training across different tasks is intended to support generalization to new members of that collection. The authors also investigate transfer to similar tasks outside it, combining model-based planning structure with learning across tasks.

Preliminary experiments on several simulated robotic tasks show strong performance. Although the network encodes the QMDP algorithm, it sometimes outperforms that algorithm in the reported experiments, which the authors attribute to end-to-end learning. The result illustrates how training a system containing a planning procedure can improve its behavior beyond that of the encoded procedure used on its own.
neurips-2017-qmdp-net-deep-learning-for-.tldr: QMDP-net embeds differentiable planning in a recurrent policy network and shows promising task generalization and performance in preliminary robotic simulations.

paragraphs: Training models with discrete latent variables is difficult when gradient estimates fluctuate strongly between samples. Existing approaches address this either by reducing the variance of REINFORCE with control variates or by replacing discrete variables with continuous relaxations. The latter can produce less noisy gradients but introduce bias into the estimate.

REBAR combines these ideas through a new control variate that uses a continuous relaxation while preserving an unbiased gradient estimate. The relaxation thus contributes to variance reduction without imposing the bias associated with using relaxed gradients directly. The authors also modify the relaxation so that its tightness can be adapted during training, removing that choice as a fixed hyperparameter.

On several benchmark generative modeling tasks, the method achieves state-of-the-art variance reduction in the reported comparisons. This generally translates into faster convergence and a better final log-likelihood, rather than being claimed for every case. The findings connect an estimator's statistical properties to practical improvements in learning models whose hidden variables are discrete.
neurips-2017-rebar-low-variance-unbiased.tldr: REBAR uses continuous relaxations within a control variate to reduce discrete-variable gradient variance without bias, generally improving training outcomes.

paragraphs: Ordinary differential equations describe systems whose states evolve over time, but learning their parameters and hidden states can be computationally demanding. Gradient matching offers a grid-free inference approach that can sometimes compete with numerical integration when the system is fully observed. Sparse observations and entirely unobserved variables make that approach much harder to use effectively.

This paper builds on an existing gradient matching method to develop a scalable variational inference framework. The framework infers system states and parameters simultaneously, addressing the coupled problem of determining how a system behaves and what values its unobserved states take. This focus targets situations where many existing gradient matching methods are difficult to apply or give unsatisfactory results.

The authors report computational speedups and improved accuracy, along with good performance under model misspecification in a partially observable system. Those findings support extending gradient matching to more demanding observation settings. They also offer an alternative inference route in applications where numerical integration remains common despite its substantial computational cost.
neurips-2017-scalable-variational-infere.tldr: A variational gradient matching framework jointly infers dynamical states and parameters, with reported speed and accuracy benefits under partial observability.

paragraphs: Random projections compress data by reducing its dimension, and quantizing the projected values can compress it further. This paper asks how accurately inner products and cosine similarities can be recovered from those coarsely stored projections. The question matters for nearest neighbor search and linear learning, where such comparisons are central to using the compressed representation.

The authors find that using only three to five bits per projection tends to produce an accuracy loss ranging from negligible to moderate. They propose simple recovery strategies and argue that, in most practically relevant scenarios, sophisticated recovery procedures such as maximum likelihood estimation are unnecessary. This is a qualified practical conclusion, rather than a guarantee for every possible dataset.

The proposed strategies also improve accuracy considerably over a previously studied Hamming-distance approach with comparable simplicity. The contribution therefore concerns both compression and reconstruction: coarse storage can preserve useful similarity information, and recovering it need not require a complex estimator. The reported comparison supports better accuracy without sacrificing the simplicity of the recovery procedure.
neurips-2017-simple-strategies-for-recov.tldr: Simple estimators recover useful inner products from projections stored with three to five bits, often making more elaborate recovery unnecessary.

paragraphs: Variational inference learns an approximate posterior by optimizing a lower bound on the model evidence. The gradient used for this optimization is often estimated from samples, so its noise can affect the learning process. This paper proposes a simple modification to the standard reparameterized gradient estimator for that objective.

The modification removes the part of the total derivative associated with the score function. Despite dropping that term, the resulting gradient estimator remains unbiased. Its variance approaches zero as the approximate posterior approaches the exact posterior. This conditional property is the central result: increasingly accurate posterior approximation is accompanied by vanishing gradient noise in the stated limit.

The authors examine the estimator both theoretically and empirically, and extend the construction to more complex variational distributions, including mixtures and importance-weighted posteriors. The contribution is a change to gradient estimation that preserves the target gradient in expectation while improving its behavior near an exact posterior. The extensions broaden the range of variational representations to which the idea can apply.
neurips-2017-sticking-the-landing-simple.tldr: Removing a score-function term yields an unbiased variational gradient estimator whose variance vanishes as the approximate posterior becomes exact.

paragraphs: This paper studies a class of nonconvex stochastic optimization problems called variationally coherent problems. The class extends beyond pseudoconvex, quasiconvex, and star-convex problems. Its purpose is to identify a weaker structural condition under which a familiar optimization method can still converge globally despite the absence of convexity.

The method is stochastic mirror descent, a family that includes stochastic gradient descent. The authors show that its last iterate converges to the solution set with probability one for the problems covered by their analysis. Focusing on the last iterate makes the claim about the sequence of actual optimization outputs, rather than only an average of earlier outputs.

The result establishes variational coherence as a sufficient condition for this convergence, showing that the stronger named convexity-related properties are not essential. It does not assert convergence for arbitrary nonconvex problems. The paper also characterizes convergence rates for the more restrictive strongly variationally coherent subclass and presents simulations, separating the general convergence result from the stronger structure used for rate guarantees.
neurips-2017-stochastic-mirror-descent-i.tldr: Variational coherence suffices for almost-sure convergence of stochastic mirror descent's last iterate, extending global convergence beyond several convexity-related classes.

paragraphs: The classical Glivenko-Cantelli theorem describes how an empirical cumulative distribution function approaches the true distribution uniformly. This paper derives a variant that gives tighter convergence bounds near extreme values of the cumulative distribution function. It then applies the result to learning revenues from observed valuations.

For revenue learning, the authors obtain sample-complexity bounds describing how quickly empirical revenues approach true revenues uniformly. These bounds assume a bound on the kth moment of valuations, with k allowed to be any real value greater than one, including fractional values. The moment condition is therefore an explicit part of the finite-sample guarantee.

The paper also gives a complete characterization of uniform convergence in the limit. If valuations have a finite first moment, uniform convergence occurs almost surely; if the first moment is infinite, it almost surely does not occur. This zero-one law identifies a precise dividing line for eventual convergence, while the higher-moment results provide quantitative control over how much data is needed.
neurips-2017-submultiplicative-glivenko-.tldr: Sharper distribution convergence bounds yield revenue-learning sample guarantees and characterize almost-sure uniform convergence by finiteness of the first valuation moment.

paragraphs: Obtaining large image datasets with reliable labels is expensive, while cheaper annotations may contain mistakes. This paper develops a framework for training deep convolutional networks from such noisy labels. It treats the observed annotation and the underlying clean label as distinct quantities whose relationship should be modeled during learning.

The framework uses an undirected graphical model to connect noisy labels with latent clean labels and trains it in a semi-supervised setting. Inference over the clean labels is tractable, and auxiliary information regularizes that inference during training. This makes the estimation of cleaner supervision part of the training process rather than simply accepting every supplied annotation as correct.

The authors apply the method to image labeling on CIFAR-10 and MS COCO. They report effectiveness both in predicting labels for previously unseen images and in reducing noise in the training labels. These two outcomes address complementary parts of the problem: learning a useful image predictor and improving the uncertain supervision from which that predictor is learned.
neurips-2017-toward-robustness-against-l.tldr: A semi-supervised graphical model learns latent clean labels alongside a convolutional network, improving image labeling and reducing training-label noise.

paragraphs: Density ratio estimation compares two probability distributions through the ratio of their densities. Because that ratio can be unbounded, corrupted observations can have a severe effect on its estimation, potentially driving the estimated value toward infinity. This paper addresses that sensitivity by designing an estimator that automatically identifies and trims outliers.

The proposed estimator has a convex formulation, and the authors state that its global optimum can be obtained using subgradient descent. This connects the robustness mechanism to an optimization problem with a global solution. Automatic trimming is central to the approach: the method incorporates the identification of problematic observations into estimation rather than requiring their removal beforehand.

The paper also analyzes parameter estimation error in high-dimensional settings and conducts experiments to verify the estimator's effectiveness. These contributions address both the statistical behavior of the recovered parameters and the practical usefulness of trimming. The resulting method targets the specific failure mode in which corrupted observations exert excessive influence on an otherwise useful distribution-comparison tool.
neurips-2017-trimmed-density-ratio-estim.tldr: A convex density-ratio estimator automatically trims outliers to reduce corruption sensitivity, with high-dimensional error analysis and experimental support.
